message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"08eb6bfc02b1f3bcef4fa69686c077f6896ced7da13b4864478e5b0a0f9ad86a","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-tx-class-c:lineage:66","source_registry_sha256":"73669019241a96617275447ad5e45b56c17a2d4bd395699448d85850cfc5bafb","units":[{"unit_id":"sec06-u01","module_id":"sec06-m01","objective_ids":["sec06-u01"],"title":{"text":"Signaling and keeping right","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01","sec06-F02"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Signals tell other drivers what you are about to do, so they can plan around you instead of guessing.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01"]},{"text":"Keeping right, and staying off the left side where you cannot see, keeps you out of the path of oncoming traffic.","fact_ids":["sec06-F02"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Ana plans to pull away from the curb and then change lanes a block later.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Pulling out from a curb and changing lanes are both signal occasions, each signaled a full one hundred feet ahead and canceled after.","fact_ids":["sec06-R01","sec06-F01"]},"result":{"text":"Ana signals before pulling out, cancels, then signals again well before her lane change and cancels once she is in the new lane.","fact_ids":["sec06-R01"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a turn signal left blinking after a lane change does no harm.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01"]},"correction":{"text":"A stray signal still reads as a turn to other drivers, so you cancel it promptly after every move.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Signal at one hundred, cancel after.","fact_ids":["sec06-R01"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You are on a two-lane road about one hundred feet from a bridge and the car ahead is slow. May you pass now?","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]},"answer":{"text":"No. The left side is closed within one hundred feet of a bridge.","fact_ids":["sec06-R02"]},"rationale":{"text":"Driving on the left is forbidden within one hundred feet of intersections, rail crossings, bridges, viaducts, and tunnels, and on hills and curves.","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Telling others your plans","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"When and how to signal.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02"]},{"text":"Where the left side closes.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson opens the section on signaling, passing, and turning. Good drivers make their plans easy to read. Signals tell other drivers what you are about to do, and keeping to the right side of the road keeps you out of the way of oncoming traffic. We will look at every occasion that calls for a signal, how far ahead to signal, how to signal by hand or by brake lights, and why you cancel promptly. Then we will cover the places where you may never drive on the left side and the few cases when the left side opens for you.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"When and how to signal","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Lane changes, turns, curb pull-outs.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01"]},{"text":"Slowing, stopping, highway entry and exit.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01"]},{"text":"Lamps or hand-and-arm signals.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"You signal every lane change, every turn, every time you pull away from a curb, every time you slow down or stop, every highway entry or exit, and every time you pull over to the side of the road. Use your signal lamps, or clear hand-and-arm signals from the window, and keep the lamps working so they show in the dark. Tapping the brake pedal so the brake lights flash warns drivers behind you that you are stopping. Signal a full one hundred feet before the move, and cancel the signal promptly afterward, because a stray signal still tells others you are turning.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Keep right; left side limits","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Keep right except to pass.","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]},{"text":"No left side near crossings, bridges.","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]},{"text":"No left side on hills, curves.","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Drive on the right side of the road except to pass. The left side is closed under no-passing markings or signs, on roads with two or more lanes each way, within one hundred feet of an intersection, a railroad crossing, a bridge, a viaduct, or a tunnel, and on hills, curves, and other places where you cannot see ahead. The left side opens when you pass on a two-lane or three-lane street, when you drive on a one-way road, or when the right side is blocked. Outside those cases, keep to the right, where oncoming drivers expect you to be.","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Closed or open left","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02","sec06-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Closed: within one hundred feet of structures.","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02","sec06-R01"]},{"text":"Closed: hills, curves, blind spots.","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02","sec06-R01"]},{"text":"Open: passing, one-way, blocked right.","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02","sec06-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from the left-side rules. The same distance, one hundred feet, shows up in two rules, and learners mix them up. You signal one hundred feet before a move, and the left side is closed within one hundred feet of intersections, rail crossings, bridges, viaducts, and tunnels. The left side is also closed on hills, curves, and anywhere you cannot see far enough ahead. It opens only for a legal pass, on a one-way road, or when the right side is blocked. When a question asks if you may move left, first check what is ahead within one hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02","sec06-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the bridge pass","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02","sec06-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Slow car, bridge ahead.","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02","sec06-F01"]},{"text":"May you pass now?","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02","sec06-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are on a two-lane road about one hundred feet from a bridge, and the car ahead of you is moving slowly. May you pass it now? Work out your answer before reading on. No, you may not. Driving on the left side is forbidden within one hundred feet of a bridge, just as it is near intersections, rail crossings, viaducts, and tunnels, and on hills and curves. Wait until you are past the bridge and have a clear view ahead, then signal a full one hundred feet before you move left to pass. Check the road ahead before you ever move left.","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02","sec06-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Signaling and lanes in brief","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01","sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Signal every move one hundred feet ahead.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01","sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]},{"text":"Cancel signals promptly.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01","sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]},{"text":"Keep right; left closes near structures.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01","sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us sum up. Signal every lane change, turn, curb pull-out, slowdown or stop, highway entry or exit, and roadside pull-over, using lamps or clear hand-and-arm signals. Keep your lamps working for the dark, tap your brakes to warn of a stop, signal a full one hundred feet ahead, and cancel promptly. Keep right except to pass. The left side is closed under no-passing markings, on roads with two or more lanes each way, within one hundred feet of intersections, rail crossings, bridges, viaducts, and tunnels, and on hills and curves. Next, how to pass safely on a two-lane road.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01","sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec06-u02","module_id":"sec06-m02","objective_ids":["sec06-u02"],"title":{"text":"Passing on a two-lane road","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03","sec06-F04"]},"why_how":[{"text":"A pass puts you in the lane of oncoming traffic, so a mistake can lead to a head-on crash.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03"]},{"text":"Following clear steps for each pass gives you enough room and time to get back safely.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Leo wants to pass a slow tractor on a two-lane road and sees an oncoming car about a quarter mile away.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Oncoming traffic must be more than two hundred feet away when the pass would end, with room to regain the right lane.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F04"]},"result":{"text":"Leo checks his mirror and blind spot, signals left, passes, waits to see the tractor in his mirror, signals right, and returns.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking you can return to your lane as soon as your car is ahead of the one you passed.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},"correction":{"text":"Wait until you can see the passed car in your mirror, then signal right and return.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F04"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"See it in the mirror, then return.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You are passing on a two-lane road and wonder when it is safe to pull back right. What is your cue?","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},"answer":{"text":"When you can see the car you passed in your rearview mirror.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04"]},"rationale":{"text":"The passed car must appear in your mirror before you signal right and return, and oncoming traffic must stay beyond two hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F04"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Passing with care","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Safe passing habits.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-F04"]},{"text":"The two-lane pass, step by step.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Passing is one of the riskiest things you do as a driver, because for a short time you are in the lane meant for oncoming traffic. This lesson covers the habits that make every pass safer and the step-by-step way to pass on a two-lane road. You will learn how much room you need from oncoming traffic, how to check your mirrors and blind spot, when to use your horn, and the exact cue that tells you it is safe to return to your lane. Take each step in order, and never start a pass you are not sure you can finish safely.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Safe passing habits","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Wait for a clear road.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03"]},{"text":"Signal and tap the horn.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03"]},{"text":"Return gently to your lane.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Every safe pass starts with waiting until the road ahead is clear. Signal your lane change so others know your plan. A light tap of the horn can warn the driver you are passing, so they are not surprised. When you return to your lane, do it gently, without cutting in sharply. The handbook gives the reason plainly: a botched pass can turn into a head-on crash, and head-on crashes are often deadly. So each habit is about the same goal, giving you and everyone around you enough room, time, and warning to stay safe while you are in the other lane.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Starting a two-lane pass","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Keep a safe following distance.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},{"text":"Check mirrors and blind spot.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},{"text":"Signal left before moving.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"On a two-lane road, begin from a safe following distance behind the car you want to pass, not tucked up close to its bumper. Check your mirrors and your blind spot, then signal left. Before you move out, make sure there are no no-passing markings or signs, and that you have enough room to get back into the right lane before oncoming traffic comes within two hundred feet. If you are not sure there is enough room, do not start the pass. A light tap of the horn can warn the other driver as you pull alongside. Patience before a pass is always the safer choice.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Finishing the pass","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pass on the left.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},{"text":"Wait for the car in your mirror.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},{"text":"Signal right, return, and cancel.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Pass on the left, keeping a steady speed. Do not return to your lane just because your car has moved ahead of the other one. Wait until you can see the car you passed in your rearview mirror. That is your cue that you have enough space. Then signal right, move back into the right lane, and cancel your signal. Throughout the pass, keep watching oncoming traffic until you are fully back in your own lane. A pass is only complete when you are fully back in your lane with your signal off and a safe gap behind you. Then settle back to a steady speed.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Start gap and return cue","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F04","sec06-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Start: oncoming beyond two hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F04","sec06-R03"]},{"text":"Return: passed car in your mirror.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F04","sec06-R03"]},{"text":"Not when your bumper clears.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F04","sec06-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from the two key moments of a pass. Before you start, oncoming traffic must be far enough away that you can get back into your lane before it comes within two hundred feet. Before you return, you must see the passed car in your rearview mirror. Learners sometimes return as soon as their front bumper clears the other car, or they confuse the two hundred feet with the one hundred feet used for signaling. When a question asks when you may start, think of the oncoming gap. When it asks when you may return, think of the mirror.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F04","sec06-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the return cue","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F04","sec06-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Mid-pass on a two-lane road.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F04","sec06-F03"]},{"text":"When do you return?","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F04","sec06-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are in the middle of passing a car on a two-lane road. What is your cue that it is safe to pull back into the right lane? Work out your answer before reading on. Your cue is seeing the car you passed in your rearview mirror. Then you signal right, move back gently, and cancel your signal. Before you even started this pass, you needed enough room to return before oncoming traffic came within two hundred feet. If that gap is shrinking, finish only if you safely can. Patience keeps every pass safe.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F04","sec06-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Passing in brief","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03","sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Clear road, signal, horn, gentle return.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03","sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},{"text":"Oncoming traffic beyond two hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03","sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},{"text":"Return when the car shows in your mirror.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03","sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, pass only when the road is clear, signal your lane change, tap the horn to avoid surprises, and return gently, because botched passes can turn head-on and deadly. On a two-lane road, start from a safe following distance, check mirrors and your blind spot, signal left, and confirm there are no no-passing markings and enough room to get back before oncoming traffic comes within two hundred feet. Pass on the left, wait to see the passed car in your mirror, signal right, return, and cancel. Next, passing on the right and being passed.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03","sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec06-u03","module_id":"sec06-m03","objective_ids":["sec06-u03"],"title":{"text":"Passing on the right","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-R05","sec06-F06"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Passing on the right is allowed only in the places the handbook lists, and only when it is safe.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05"]},{"text":"Both drivers share the job of a safe pass: the passed driver holds steady and the passer does not linger.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"On a two-lane road, Dee is behind a car stopped to turn left, and there is a paved shoulder on the right.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-R05"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Right-side passing is lawful on a paved shoulder past a left-turning vehicle when it is safe, but never by leaving the pavement.","fact_ids":["sec06-R05","sec06-F05"]},"result":{"text":"Dee checks that it is safe and passes on the paved shoulder, staying on the pavement the whole time.","fact_ids":["sec06-R05"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking it is fine to drive onto the dirt beside the road to get around a turning car.","fact_ids":["sec06-R05"]},"correction":{"text":"Right-side passes may use a paved shoulder, but you may never pass by leaving the pavement.","fact_ids":["sec06-R05","sec06-F05"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Right passes stay on the pavement.","fact_ids":["sec06-R05"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You notice you have been driving in another car's blind spot for a while. What should you do?","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-R06"]},"answer":{"text":"Finish the pass or drop back out of the blind spot.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06"]},"rationale":{"text":"Passers never linger in blind spots; they complete the pass or fall back out of sight.","fact_ids":["sec06-R06","sec06-F06"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Right passes and being passed","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"When the right side is allowed.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06"]},{"text":"Duties of both drivers.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers the other side of passing. First, the few situations in which you may pass on the right, and the one thing you may never do when passing on that side. Then we turn to what happens when someone passes you. A pass is safest when both drivers do their part, and the handbook gives each driver a clear job. The passed driver keeps things steady, and the passing driver avoids lingering where they cannot be seen. Knowing both roles helps you whether you are the one passing or the one being passed on the road.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"When right-side passing is lawful","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Clear, wide multi-lane roads.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-R05"]},{"text":"One-way roads.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-R05"]},{"text":"Paved shoulders past stopped or turning cars.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Passing on the right is lawful only when it is safe and only in certain places. You may pass on the right on clear, wide roads with more than one lane in your direction, on one-way roads, and along paved shoulders when the vehicle ahead is slowing, stopped, disabled, or turning left. In every case, you must stay on the pavement. Passing by driving off the pavement onto dirt or grass is never allowed. So the right side is a narrow exception, not an everyday choice, and you use it only when the road and the situation clearly allow it to be done safely.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Being passed and passing","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Passed driver: hold speed and lane.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-R06"]},{"text":"Ease right on unmarked lanes.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-R06"]},{"text":"Passer: finish or fall back.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"When another car passes you, hold your speed and stay in your lane. On a road without lane markings, ease to the right to give the passing car more room, and generally make its path smooth rather than harder. Do not speed up to block the pass. When you are the one passing, never linger in the other driver's blind spot. Either complete the pass or fall back far enough that the other driver can see you. Lingering alongside another car keeps you out of the other driver's sight, which is what the rule is meant to prevent.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-R06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Paved shoulder or off the road","fact_ids":["sec06-R05","sec06-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Paved shoulder past a stopped car: allowed.","fact_ids":["sec06-R05","sec06-F05"]},{"text":"Leaving the pavement: never.","fact_ids":["sec06-R05","sec06-F05"]},{"text":"Only when it is safe.","fact_ids":["sec06-R05","sec06-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from the right-side rules. The handbook allows you to pass on a paved shoulder when the vehicle ahead is slowing, stopped, disabled, or turning left. But it never allows you to pass by leaving the pavement. Learners sometimes treat any space to the right as fair game, including dirt or gravel beside the road. It is not. A second trap is thinking a right pass is allowed simply because the driver ahead is slow. Slowness alone is not enough. The road must be one where right passes are allowed, and it must be safe.","fact_ids":["sec06-R05","sec06-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the blind spot","fact_ids":["sec06-R06","sec06-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Beside another car for a while.","fact_ids":["sec06-R06","sec06-F06"]},{"text":"What should you do?","fact_ids":["sec06-R06","sec06-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you realize you have been driving beside another car, in its blind spot, for a while. What should you do? Work out your answer before reading on. Either finish the pass or drop back out of the blind spot, so the other driver can see you. Never linger there. If you were the driver being passed instead, your job would be to hold your speed and lane, ease right on a road without lane markings, and make the passing car's path smooth. Both drivers together make the pass safe. Check the road type and the conditions first.","fact_ids":["sec06-R06","sec06-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Right passes in brief","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-R05","sec06-F06","sec06-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Right passes only where allowed and safe.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-R05","sec06-F06","sec06-R06"]},{"text":"Never leave the pavement.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-R05","sec06-F06","sec06-R06"]},{"text":"Hold steady; never linger.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-R05","sec06-F06","sec06-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us sum up. Passing on the right is lawful only when safe on clear, wide multi-lane roads, on one-way roads, or along paved shoulders past vehicles that are slowing, stopped, disabled, or turning left, and never by leaving the pavement.
